glance: 100 km to Brahmanbaria by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
arifail-mosque.desc: The Arifail mosque in Sarail upazila is a fine example of Mughal-period mosque architecture in eastern Bengal, with domes over a rectangular prayer hall. It is protected as an archaeological monument. Its rural setting makes it a peaceful stop.
blocks: How to get there
From Brahmanbaria town take a CNG to Sarail (about 30 minutes), then a local rickshaw to Arifail.
Good to know
It is an active mosque; avoid prayer times and dress modestly.

glance: 100 km to Brahmanbaria by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
ulchapara-mosque.desc: The Ulchapara Jame Mosque stands in Ulchapara village in Brahmanbaria Sadar. An inscription dates it to 1727–28, and it was founded by a merchant from the west, Shah Muhammad Murad, whose grave lies beside it. The original building had no verandah; later additions have been made, but the old prayer hall still stands. It is a protected archaeological site that few visitors to the town ever see.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or auto from Brahmanbaria town to Ulchapara, a short ride.
Good to know
Visit outside prayer times and dress modestly.

ustad-alauddin-khan-heritage.desc: Ustad Alauddin Khan, born in Shibpur in Brahmanbaria, became one of the most influential figures in Hindustani classical music, the teacher of Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan and many others. His brother Ustad Ayet Ali Khan, also from Shibpur, was a renowned musician and instrument maker. The district remembers them with a music academy in town and festivals of classical and folk music, keeping a strong local tradition of musical training alive.

glance: 100 km to Brahmanbaria by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
kalbhairab-temple.desc: The Kalbhairab temple in the Medda area of Brahmanbaria town is known for its very tall image of Kalbhairab, among the largest such idols in the country. The temple has deep roots in local devotion and draws large gatherings during its annual festivals. Even outside festival days, the scale of the image inside the sanctum is striking.
blocks: How to get there
In Brahmanbaria town; a short rickshaw ride from the railway station.
Good to know
Remove shoes and dress modestly. Ask before taking photos inside.

kharampur-mazar-sharif.desc: The shrine is the resting place of Syed Ahmad Gesudaraz, remembered as one of the 360 followers who came to Sylhet with Hazrat Shah Jalal in 1303. Local tradition says fishermen on the Titas river found a severed head in their net, which spoke to them; they converted and buried it here, and their descendants became the shrine's keepers. Historians link this to a battle in the kingdom of Taraf, in which he is thought to have fallen. The shrine stands on large grounds near the Titas, and its yearly Urs draws devotees from across the region.
blocks: How to get there
Train or bus to Akhaura, then a CNG or auto to Kharampur.
Good to know
During the Urs the roads and grounds are packed; go on another day for a calmer visit. Dress modestly and cover your head inside the shrine.

glance: Old sweet shops in Brahmanbaria town such as Adarsha Matri Bhandar and Mahadev Mishtanna Bhandar
brahmanbaria-chhanamukhi.desc: Chhanamukhi is made by pressing fresh chhana into a block, cutting it into small cubes, frying them and then cooking them in syrup until a dry, sugary coat forms. The result is chewy inside and crisp outside, quite unlike the syrupy sweets of most districts. It takes several litres of milk to make one kilogram, which keeps it special. In 2024 it received Geographical Indication status as a product of Brahmanbaria.

glance: Rice hotels near Brahmanbaria town bazar and river ghats
titas-river-fish.desc: Brahmanbaria's rivers and haor wetlands supply a steady catch of freshwater fish such as rui, boal, ayre, pabda and small mixed fish. Local cooks favour light jhol curries with potato or seasonal vegetables, and crisp fried small fish with rice. The best place to taste it is at modest hotels near the river ghats and bazars.

glance: 100 km to Brahmanbaria by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
titas-river.desc: The Titas loops around Brahmanbaria town on its way to the Meghna. In the rainy season it swells wide and the banks fill with boats, fishing nets and children swimming. Its fame comes from Adwaita Mallabarman's novel 'Titas Ekti Nadir Naam', about a fishing community on its banks, later filmed by Ritwik Ghatak. A hired country boat at sunset is the best way to see it.
blocks: How to get there
From Brahmanbaria town, ask a rickshaw to take you to a ghat on the Titas and hire a boat there.
Good to know
Agree the boat fare before setting off. Wear a life jacket if one is available.

sarail-hatirpul.desc: Hatirpul, the 'elephant bridge', is an old brick bridge in Sarail, linked in local tradition with the dewans of Sarail who kept elephants. It is weathered and modest, but it is one of the few surviving structures from that period in the area. It pairs easily with a visit to Arifail mosque.
blocks: How to get there
In Sarail upazila; local rickshaw drivers know it.
Good to know
Treat the structure gently and do not climb on it.

glance: 100 km to Brahmanbaria by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
haripur-zamindar-bari.desc: Haripur Barabari stands on the east bank of the Titas in Haripur union of Nasirnagar upazila, about 15 km from Nasirnagar on the way to Madhabpur. The Roy Choudhury zamindars built a three-storey palace with dozens of rooms, a durbar hall, temples, a pond and a wide brick ghat stepping down to the river, flanked by memorial towers. The family left for India after 1947, and the building is now weathered and partly ruined. In the rainy season water spreads all around, and the palace with its reflection is a favourite of photographers and film crews.
blocks: How to get there
From Brahmanbaria town go by bus or CNG to Nasirnagar, then take a CNG to Haripur; in the monsoon you can also go part of the way by boat.
Good to know
Parts of the building are unsafe; do not climb the broken stairs or upper floors. People still live in some sections, so be respectful.
